Defining Poverty Line 
*384.SHRI EKANATH K. THAKUR: Will the Minister of URBAN 
EMPLOYMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be pleased to state: 
 whether it is a fact that there are serious flaws in the methodology 
adopted by Government in defining poverty line as it makes very little 
provision for other essentials of life like drinking water, shelter and 
sanitation; 
 whether it is a fact that the rate of decline of poverty since 1973 has been at 
dismal 0.81 per cent per annum and the number of poor stood at about 25 crore 
in 2004; and 
 if so, the steps Government propose to take to include parameters like 
drinking water, shelter etc., in the definition of poverty? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF URBAN 
EMPLOYMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (KUMARI SELJA): (a) to 
(c) The methodology adopted by the Planning Commission, Government of India, 
in defining the poverty line is as recommended by the Expert Group on 
"Estimation of Proportion of Number of Poor" (Lakdawala Committee) and is 
widely acknowledged to be one of the most sophisticated met hodologies. 
Based on this expert group report, the Planning Commission has adopted a Per 
Capita Consumption Expenditure needed to attain the minumum amount of non-
food expenditure in order to meet the requirements of clothing, shelter, transport etc. 
as the critertion to define the poverty line. 
The Planning Commission estimates the in cidence of poverty at national 
and State level from the large sample survey on household consumer expenditure 
conducted by the National Sample survey  Organization (NSSO) at an interval 
of approximately five years according to the expert 
9 

RAJYA SABHA  [11 May, 2006] 
Group Medhodology. On the basis of this methodology, incidence of proverty was 
calculated for the years 1973-74, 1977-78, 1983-84, 1987-88, 1993-94 and 
1999-2000, when the data from the results of large scale sample suvery by 
National Sample Survey Organization on Household Consumer Expenditure 
were available. It is observed from the estimates made by the Planning 
Commission that the incidence of poverty has declined from 56.4 percent in 
1973-74 to 27.1 percent in 1999-2000. The poverty rate defined as the percentage 
of the poor has declined at a rate of 1.13% points per year between 1973-74 and 
1999-2000 and the annual average rate at which the total number of poor 
people has declined is 0.81 per cent during this period. 
The next estimate of poverty by the Planning Commission will be based on the 
results of 61st round of NSS conducted during 2004-05, which is yet to be 
published. Therefore, the question of the number of poor during 2004 at about 
25 crore, does not arise. 
There is no proposal with the Planning Commission to evolve a new 
definition of poverty line including parameters like drinking water, shelter, etc. 
Insofar as the Ministry of Urban Employnment & Poverty Alleviation is 
concerned, for identification of genuine beneficiaries under the Swarna Jayanti 
Shahari Rozgar Yojana (SJSRY), both economic and non-economic parameters are 
considered. Based on the State specific urban poverty lines, as estimated by 
the Planning Commission, the below poverty line (BPL) survery is made by the 
States/Union Territories. The non-economic parameters, like shelter, water, 
sanitation, etc., are then applied to this urban below poverty line (BPL) 
population for identification of genuine beneficiaries under the Scheme.

Handing over of Kachatheevu Island to Sri Lanka 
*396. SHRI T.T.V. DHINAKARAN: Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to 
state: 
 whether it is a fact that Kachatheevu Island was given to Sri Lanka under 
an Agreement; 
 if so, the details of the Agreement; 
 whether Sri Lanka has been abiding by the Agreement so far; and 
 the consequences that would follow in the event of Sri Lanka violating the 
Agreement? 
22 

[11 May, 2006]   RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNALAFFAIRS 
(SHRIE. AHAMMED): (a) and (b) Kachatheevu Island lies on the Sri Lankan side of 
the India-Sri Lanka International maritime Boundary Line (IMBL). The IMBL 
was settled by a 1974 Agreement demarcating it in the Palk Straits and a 
subsequent Agreement in 1976 demarcating it in the Gulf of Mannar and Bay of 
Bengal. These agreements were subsequently laid before Parliament. Under the 
Agreement, Indian fishermen are allowed access to Kachatheevu Island for rest, 
for drying of nets and for the Annual St. Anthony's festival. The right of access 
is not understood to cover fishing rights around the island to Indian 
fishermen. 
(c) and (d) Access to Kachatheevu Island for Indian fishermen was 
suspended by Sri Lankan Government in 1983 due to security concerns and was 
restored in 2003 after normalization of the situation. Sri Lankan Government is, 
therefore, not in violation of the above Agreement. Should, however, Sri Lanka 
not abide by the Agreement, the matter will be raised by the Government of

Long term energy security 
2711. SHRI BALAVANT ALIAS BAL APTE: Will the PRIME MINISTER 
be pleased to state: 
 whether the Government have rece ntly formulated a nuclear power 
programme to provide long-term energy security to the country based on 
indigenous nuclear fuel resources; 
 if so, the details thereof; and 
 the stage at which it stands at present? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE PRIME MINISTER'S OFFICE (SHRI 
PRITHVIRAJ CHAVAN): (a) A three-stage nuclear power programme to 
utilize large thorium reserves in the country for electricity generation has been 
envisaged since the inception of nuclear power-programme in the country. 
(b) The three stages of the programme are: 
 Pressurised Heavy Reactors (PHWR) in the first stage, based on natural 
uranium available in the country. 
 Fast Breeder Reactors (FBR) utilising plutonium-uranium fuel 
cycle, in the second stage. 
 Reactors for utilisation of our vast resources of thorium, in the third 
stage. 
The three stages have important fuel cycle linkages and have to be gone 
through sequentially. 
26 

[11 May, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) At present there are 15(13 PHWRs and 2 Boiling Water Reactors) power 
reactor in operation with  a total capacity of 3360 MWe. In addition, five 
Pressurised Heavy Water Reactors (PHW Rs) and two Light Water Reactors 
(LWRs) are under construction. 
A beginning to the second stage programme has been made with the start of 
construction of 500 MWe Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor (PFBR) at 
Kalpakkam, Tamil Nadu. 
The third stage of the programme will be launched after sufficient base 
capacity of the second stage FBRs are put in operation. A technology 
demonstration project -Advanced Heavy Water Reactor (AHWR) is planned for 
construction to move forward on technologies for Thorium utilisation and 
innovative reactor systems. A small research reactor Kalpakkam Mini Reactor 
(KAMINI) of third stage is already in operation.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS (SHRI ANAND SHARMA): (a) to (e) Following the terrorist attacks in 
the United States on September 11,2001, the United Nations Security Council 
adopted Resolution 1373 on September 28,2001 under Chapter VII of the UN 
Charter. This resolution places binding obligations on all Member States to 
combat terrorism in ail its forms and manifestations, and requires them to take 
various measures in this context. A Counter Terrorism Committee (CTC) was

the CTC and the steps taken and planned to implement Resolution 1373. 
Government of India has submitted four reports to the CTC, in December 2001, 
July 2002, March 2003 and May 2004, respectively. In these reports, the 
Government has furnished details of several counter-terrorism measures taken by it to 
deny all forms of financial support to terrorist groups; suppress the provision of 
safe haven, sustenance or support to terrorists, share information with other 
governments on any groups practicing or planning terrorist acts; co-operate 
with other governments in the investigation, detection, arrest and prosecution of 
those involved in such acts; criminalise assistance for terrorism and bring 
violators of the law to justice. 
These reports have been prepared in consultation and coordination with the 
Ministry of Home Affairs and other relevant Ministries/Departments of the 
Government.

Three-tier Panchayati Raj System 
†2779. SHRI DILIP SINGH JUDEV: Will the Minister of PANCHAYATI 
RAJ be pleased to state: 
 the States where three-tier elected Panchayati Raj System has not been 
implemented as on 31st January, 2006; 
 the reasons therefor; 
 the action proposed to be taken against these States; and 
 the details of the action taken for implementation of three tier 
Panchayati Raj System? 
THE MINISTER OF PANCHAYATI RAJ (SHRI MANi SHANKARA1YAR); 
(a) to (d) As per the Constitution (73rd Amendment) Act, 1992, the three Tier 
Panchayat System is in place at the Village, Intermediate and District levels in the 
States having population of above 20 lakhs. In the States where the population 
is less than 20 lakhs, Intermediate Panchayats are 
†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
93 

RAJYA SABHA [11 May, 2006] 
not necessarily to be constituted. As per this provision, the Panchayati Raj 
System has been implemented in all the States with installation of Panchayati 
Raj Institutions through timely held elections, except in Jharkhand, where 
elections are pending as the matter relating to reservation of posts is sub-judice. In 
Pondicherry, Panchayat elections are pending for want of information from the 
Office of the Registrar General of India pertaining to village panchayat-wise 
population, for notifying the same for the purpose of allotment and rotation of 
seats and offices in Panchayats by the State Election Commission. In respect of 
other States, it may be mentioned that while the provisions of 73rd (Amendment) 
Act, 1992 do not apply in the States of Meghalaya, Mizoram and Nagaland, the 
State of Jammu & Kashmir is yet to adopt the 73rd (Amendment) Act, 1992.

Raj has been impressing upon the defaulting States from time to time to put in 
place elected Panchayati Raj Institutions.

as institutions of self-government, as envisaged in Part IX of the Constitution, the 
Ministry of Panchayati Raj convened Seven Round Tables of State Ministers of

formulated by consensus. Inter alia, these cover points of action pertaining to 
both the Centre and the States, relating to the effective devolution of functions, 
funds and functionaries to Panchayats, strengthening Gram Sabhas, planning 
and implementation by Panchayats, reservations, implementation of Panchayats

Union Secretary (Panchayati Raj) have been

constituted to monitor the progre ss on the implementation of the 150

functionaries, activity mapping, constitution of District Planning Committees, 
implementation of PESA, capacity building of elected members of Panchayats, IT 
enabled e-govemance at Panchayat level have been discussed with States. 
With a view to interact with Panchayats and carrying out a review with

around follow up measures on activity mapping, matching transfer of funds 
and functionaries, creation of Panchayat sector in the State budget, 
constitution and operational guidelines for District Planning Committee 
within an agreed time frame. 
An exercise is underway to review different statutes with a view to

Panchayati Raj had constituted an expert group to study and make

 Yes, sir. The performance across th e States in taking appropriate

2784. SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH:  Will the PRIME MINISTER be

Yes, Sir. 
 Section 12(7) of the Right to Information Act, 2005 provides that the 
Headquarters of the Central Information Commission (CIC) shall be at Delhi 
and the CIC may, with the previous approval of the Central Government, 
establish offices at other places in I ndia. The CIC has not yet proposed for 
establishing offices at other places. 
 According to Rule 7(2) of the Central Information Commission (Appeal

hearing may or may not be held, depending upon the facts and circumstances of the 
case. As far as possible, CIC does not postpone its hearing.

BPL people in Orissa 
2796.   MS. PRAMILABOHIDAR: 
SHRI B.J. PANDA: 
Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to state: 
 whether it is a fact that around 260 million of the people are still below 
poverty line, the highest number being in Orissa, as per the country's first social 
development report; and 
 if so, what is Government's action plan to help the cash-strapped State to 
improve its social development sector to control the high rate of BPL in the 
State? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING 
(SHRI M.V. RAJASEKHARAN): (a) As per the recent report brought out by 
the Council for Social Development, published by Oxford University Press, 
namely, 'India Social Development Report", it has been stated-that 260 million 
Indians are still below poverty line according to 1999-2000 data (page No. 2, Table 
No. 1.1. of the Report). The Report also indicates that 
108 

[11 May, 2006] RAJ YA SABHA 
the highest percentage of people below the poverty line is in Orissa. It may be 
mentioned that these figures are taken from the official poverty estimates 
brought out by the Planning Commission on the basis of NSS 55th round of 
large scale sample survey on household consumer expenditure, which was 
conducted during the year 1999-2000. As per the official estimates, the highest 
number of people helow the poverty line is in Bihar. 
(b) The Government has been implementing various programmes/schemes through 
out the country including Orissa to help improve its social development sector to reduce 
the number of people below poverty line. 
In rural areas, the programmes which are being implemented by the 
Ministry of Rural Development for upliftment of BPL families are (i) 
Sampoorna Grameen Rozgar Yojana (SGRY), (ii) Swaranjayati Gram 
Swarozgar Yojana (SGSY), (iii) IndiraAwas Yojana (IAY), and (iv) National 
Rural Employment Guarantee Act. 
It may be noted that NREGS has been launched in 19 districts of Orissa with 
effect from 2nd Feb. 2006. 
The poverty alleviation programme which is being implemented in urban areas is 
Swarra Jayanti Shahari Rozgar Yojana (SJSRY). This programme seeks to provide 
gainful employment to the urban unemployed or underemployed poor 
through setting up of micro enterprises and also through provision of Wage 
Employment by utilizing their labour for construction of useful public assets. 
Jawaharlal Nehru National Urban Renewal Mission (JNNURM) and Integrated 
Housing and Slum Development Programme (IHSDP) are being implemented to 
provide shelter for urban slum dwellers in 6.3 selected cities and remaining urban 
areas respectively. 
The Public Distribution System in India has been more focused and 
targeted towards the very poor category. The "Antyodaya Anna Yojana" 
provides 35 kgs of foodgrains to the poorest of the poor families at a highly 
subsidized rate of Rs. 2 per kg., for wheat and Rs. 3 per kg, for rice. 
Recently, the coverage of Antyodaya Anna Yojana has been expanded from 
2.0 crore (BPL) families to 2.5 crore families in 2005. The State Governments 
have been advised to give priority to the households from the poorest and the 
backward blocks and/or where nutritional deficiency is more widespread, 
while identifying the beneficiaries. 
109 

RAJYA SABHA [11 May, 2006] 
In addition to the above national programmes, the Rashtriya Sam Vikas Yojana 
(RSVY) is also being implemented in Orissa. Under the Backward Districts 
Initiative component of RSVY, five districts of Orissa, namely, Keonjhar, 
Sundergarh, Ganjam, Gajapati and Mayurbhanj are covered for which Special 
Central Assistance of Rs. 45 crore for each district is to be provided over a period 
of three years. Under another component of RSVY, namely Special Plan for the 
undivided Kalahandi - Bolangir - Koraput (KBK) disricts of Orissa, Special Central 
Assistance of Rs. 250 crore per annum is being provided during the Tenth Plan 
period.

Growth rate of GDP 
2800. SHRI S. S. AHLUWALIA: Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to 
state: 
 whether a year-on-year growth rate of 8 to 10 per cent in GDP is being 
targeted; 
 if so, the details of the sectors of the economy expected to contribute thereto 
most and in what manner; 
 the broad relation between GDP growth rate and poverty alleviation in the 
context of Indian economy; 
 in what manner the targeted growth rate can be achieved in the present 
political scenario; and 
 its proposed impact on alleviation of poverty? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING (SHRI 
M.V. RAJASEKHARAN): (a) The Tenth Five Year Plan (2002-07) had set a target 
of 8.1% annual average growth rate, measured in terms of GDP at market prices. 
The targeted growth rate was revised downwards to 7% during the Mid-term 
Appraisal of the Tenth Plan. 
 The Tenth Five Year Plan had targeted to achieve a growth rate of 4.0%, 
8.9% and 9.3% for agriculture, industry and services sector, respectively. The 
Mid-term appraisal of the Tenth Plan has revised these targets to 2.2%, 7.6% and 
8.3% for the three sectors, respectively. 
 The incidence of poverty is expected to be inversely related with per-capita 
income and agricultural productivity, as indicated in the Tenth Five Year Plan 
Document. Consistent with the overall growth targets of 8.1% for GDP and 4% 
for Agriculture set for the Tenth Plan, the Plan Document has projected that the 
proportion of people living below poverty line may be expected to decline to 
19.3% at the end of the Tenth+ive Year Plan, as compared to 26.1% in 1999-
2000.

but realistic action plans at the State and district levels with 
short-term and long-term approaches and strategies to combat

development fronts.

including attempts to undermine or overthrow legitimate goverments. In 
pursuance of the resolution No. 55/56 (2000) adopted by UN General 
Assembly, the Kimberley Process was in itiated to regulate the movement 
of rough diamonds and curb trad'ng in conflict diamonds. The aim of the 
Kimberley Process is to formulate concrete proposals for a system of 
Certificate of Origin for trade in rough diamonds and for appropriate 
arrangement to ensure compliance. Af ter the Ministerial meeting held at 
Interlaken, Switzerland on 5th November, 2002, the KP Certification Scheme 
(KPCS) was launched on 1st January, 2003 including in India. 
Implementation is based on respective laws of the participating nations 
, and internal system of control meeting the standards established in the 
Documents of KPCS. Kimberley Proces s Certificate (KPC) means a forgery 
resistant document in a particular format, which identifies a shipment of 
rough diamonds as being in compliance with the requirements of the 
certification scheme. KPC accompanies each shipment of rough diamonds 
on export/import. Ther efore, the question of any conflict of opinion with 
Ministry of Mines on issue of conflict diamonds does not arise.

2568. SHRI RAJKUMAR DHOOT: Will the Minister of COMMERCE

WTO rounds of negotiations? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY (SHRI JAIRAM RAMESH): (a) to (c) A Declaration was adopted 
at the conclusion of the Sixth Ministerial Conference of the World Trade 
Organisation (WTO) held between 13 -18 December 2005 at Hong Kong. 
The Declaration stipulates that in a th ree-band structure for reducing trade- 
distorting domestic support, the Member with the highest level (EU) of 
permitted support will be in the top band with the highest cuts, the two

such developing countries that have entitlement to provide Aggregate 
Measurement of Support (AMS) will be in the lowest band with the smallest 
cuts. Furthermore, disciplines will be developed to achieve effective cuts 
in trade-distroting domestic support. Developing countries like India, with 
no commitments on reduction of Aggregate Measurement of Support would 
be exempted from reduction in their de-minims support. 
Members will negotiate the exact quantu m of cuts to be effected to the 
trade distorting domestic support as part of finalization of modalities in 
agriculture. In agriculture, ambition across the three pillars of domestic 
support, market access and export subsidies will be balanced.

2578. SHRI HARISH RAWAT: Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
whether it is a fact that due to geographical contiguity, Myanmar's 
trade with Thailand mostly passes through overland while sea routes are 
used for trading with rest of the BIMSTEC countries; 
whether it is also a fact that India has only one land route of Myanmar 
in Manipur and the volume of business through this route is low due to 
lack of infrastructure facilities and insurgency; and 
if answers to part (a) and (b) are in  affirmative, what action Government 
propose to increase the volume of tr ade between these two countries by 
circumventing the difficulties faced in Manipur? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY (SHRI JAIRAM RAMESH): (a) Yes, Sir. 
Moreh is the only land route to Myanmar in Manipur. Trade depends 
on a variety of factors including inter-alia infrastucture facilities, law and 
order situation, demand and supply of commodities etc. 
Trade promotion is a continuous and ongoing efforts of the 
Government. Several initiatives including organizing buyer-seller meets, 
participation in international faire, bu siness delegation etc. are undertaken 
to boost India's trade. Depending upon the demands of trade, initiatives 
are taken to improve infrastructure fa cilities to service the trade across 
land borders.

Assistance for tobacco exports 
2580. SHRI V. HANUMANTHA RAO: Will the Minister of COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
the specific assistance being gi ven by the Tobacco Board to 
encourage tobacco exports from Andhra Pradesh; 
the number of farmers who will benefit from such exports; 
the specific financial assistance being give., to Andhra farmers to 
grow better quality Virginia tobacco; 
whether such assistance will be increased in the coming fiscal 
year; and 
the steps proposed in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY (SHRI JAIRAM RAMESH): (a) The Tobacco Board provides 
assistance to the tobacco farmers through various extension and developmental 
schemes for improving the quality and productivity of tobacco grown in the State 
of Andhra Pradesh in tune with the changing international demands to promote 
exports. The schemes include, Farm Mechanization, Improving Yield & Quality 
of FCV tobacco, Improving curing practices, model project areas, integrated 
pest-management & quality circles etc. The Tobacco Board undertakes extensive 
advertisement campaign in the international media to promote Indian tobacco. 
All tobacco farmers are extende d assistance under these schemes 
to derive benefit from exports. 
to (e) An allocation of Rs. 85.20 lakhs has been made for the year 
2006-07 for these schemes. The Tobacco Board had also organized Input 
loans of about Rs. 30.00 crores to the farmers at 6%-6.5% rate of interest 
per annum from scheduled banks for 2005-06 crop season. The assistance 
under these schemes is extended as per need from time to time. 
Discussions on crop specific issues 
2581. SHRI V. HANUMANTHA RAO: Will the Minister of COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have invited the farmers to discuss various 
crop-specific issues pertaining to WTO and Andhra Pradesh; 
243 

RAJYA SABHA [11 May, 2006] 
if so, what are the issues raised by  the farmers with regard to Andhra 
Pradesh; 
whether any safeguards are being negotiated with WTO on cash 
crops like chillies, Virginia tobacco , turmeric etc. from Andhra Pradesh; 
and 
the steps proposed to protect farmers from the open economy and 
WTO? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY (SHRI JAIRAM RAMESH): (a) and (b) The Government have, 
in association with UNCTAD organized a series of meetings with farmer's 
organizations including NGOs to discuss WTO related issues. 
Representatives of farmer's organizations from Andhra Pradesh have also 
attended these discussions. The farmer s indicated that crude/refined edible 
oil, rice, oil seeds, sugar, groundnuts, oilcakes of cotton seed, cotton 
linters and raw cotton would require protection against tariff reductions in 
the ongoing negotiations at the WTO. 
The G-33 Group of countries, of which India is a part, have proposed 
that all agricultural products of deve loping countries should be protected 
against surge in imports and price depression. The Hong Kong Ministerial 
Conference has instructed the member s to negotiate a Special Safeguard 
Mechanism with import quantity and price triggers. 
The Government is aware of the conc erns of the Indian farmers in an 
open economy. India has maintained at the WTO that the developing 
countries cannot be asked to reduce their agriculture tariffs as long as the 
developed countries continue to subsidize the domestic produce of their 
farmers and also extend export subsidies to them. The Hong Kong Ministerial 
Declaration has already recognized the right of the developing countries to 
self-designate an appropriate number of  tariff lines as Special Products to 
meet their food security, livelihood security and rural development needs. 
The G-33 proposal indicates that on these lines, zero or a minimal tariff 
reduction is required to be undertaken in respect of Special Products. 
Developing country member will also have a right to have recourse to a 
Special Safeguard Mechanism to guard against surge in volume of imports 
and also against price depressions. The Government is committed to 
providing adequate protection to domestic producers through WTO 
244 

[11 May, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
compatible measures, including by calibrating the applied tariffs within the 
bound duties.

Anti-Dumping cases 
2590. SHRI GIREESH KUMAR SANGHI: Will the Minister of 
COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that 81 per cent of anti-dumping cases initiated in 
2003-04, provisional or final anti-dumping were recommended or imposed; 
whether it is a fact that in se veral of these cases the main 
consideration was an increase in th e share of imports from the foreign 
firms inspite of growth of sales and profits of domestic industry, and 
since growth in imports is natural with trade liberalization, what 
measures Govemment are taking to ensure that anti-dumping remedy is 
used not merely to restrict competition but of provide relief from injury? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY (SHRI JAIRAM RAMESH): (a) No, Sir. During 2003-04, Anti- 
Dumping investigations were initiated in 14 cases. Out of these, 
preliminary/final findings had been issued in 13 cases. Duty was not 
recommended in 3 cases. In one ca se the petition was withdrawn by the 
domestic industry. Measures imposed are in 10 cases. 
(b) and (c) As per the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 as amended in 1995 and 
the Rules framed, thereunder, Anti-dumping investigations are normally 
initiated by the Directorate General of Anti-Dumping and Allied Duties 
(DGAD) on receiving a fully documented petition from the domestic industry 
with prima-facie evidence of dumping, injury and casual link between the 
dumped goods and injury to the domestic industry. The purpose of Anti- 
dumping duties is to counteract trade distortion caused by dumping and 
the consequential injury to the domestic industry. Anti-dumping measures 
are taken for ensuring fair trade and is not a measure to restrict competition.

Reforms in Textile sector 
2679. SHRI B.J. PANDA: Will the Minister of TEXTILES be pleased to 
state: 
whether it is a fact that the Textiles sector needs more reforms and 
investment; 
whether the IMF has asked India to step up reforms and investment 
in this sector to bolster the sector's competitiveness; and 
if so, the action plan of the Centre to revamp and upgrade this sector 
and remove the existing constraints to boost up its exports? 
327 

RAJYA SABHA [11 May, 2006] 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF TEXTILES (SHRI 
E.V.S. ELANGOVAN): (a) to (c) Since reforms and investment are 
continuous process, the Textiles sector needs more reforms and 
investment. However, the IMF has not asked India to step up reforms and 
investment in this sector to bolster the sector's competitiveness. Certain 
important measures taken by the Government to strengthen the Indian 
Textile Sector include:— 
(i) To improve productivity and quality of cotton for manufacture and 
export of competitive downstream  textile products, Government 
has launched the Technology Mission on Cotton (TMC). 
(ii) The Technology Upgradation Fund Scheme (TUFS) was launched 
to facilitate the modernisation and upgradation of the textile 
industry both in the organised and unorganised sector. The Scheme 
has been further fine tuned to in crease the rapid investments in 
the targeted sub-sectors of the textile industry. The cost of 
machinery has been further brough t down by reducing the customs 
duty on imports. 
(iii) To provide the textile industry with world-class infrastructure 
facilities for setting up their textile units meeting international 
environmental and social standard s, a Public-Private Partnership 
(PPP) based scheme known as the "Scheme for Integrated Textile 
Park (SITP)" has been introduced in July 2005. 
(iv) In 2004-05 Budget, the entire textile sector, except for man-made 
fibre and filament yarn was provided optional exemption from excise 
duty. 
(v) To facilitate import of state of the art machinery to make our 
products internationally competitive in post quota regime, in 
2005-06 Budget, the customs duty on textile machinery has been 
brought down to 10% except 23  machinery items appearing in 
List 49 which attracts Basic customs Duty (BCD) of 15%. The 
concessional duty of 5% continues to be at 5% on most of the 
machinery items. 
(vi) In the Current Budget (2006-07), with a view to making textile 
industry more competitive:— 
328 

[11 May, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
Import duty on raw materials such as DMT, PTA and MEG has 
been reduced from 15% to 10% and for paraxylene from 5% to 2%. 
CENVAT on all man made fibre and yarn has been reduced from 
16% to 8% and import duty on all man made fibre and yarns from 
15% to 10%. 
The peak rate of ad-valorem component of customs duty for all 
non-agricultural products including textiles has been reduced from 
15% to 12.5%. 
Special CVD of 4% has been extended to all goods in order to 
counter balance various internal taxes like sales tax and VAT and 
to provide a level playing field to indigenous goods which have to 
bear these taxes. However, fabrics are exempted from this levy. 
(vii) Government has allowed 100% Fo reign Direct Investment (FDI) in 
the textile sector under automatic route. 
(viii) For speedy modernisation of the textile processing sector, 
Government has introduced a credit linked capital subsidy scheme 
@10% under TUFS, in addition to the existing 5% interest 
reimbursement. 
(ix) Government has launched the Debt Restructuring Scheme w.e.f. 
Sept., 2003 with the principal objective to permit banks to lend to 
the textile sector at 8-9% rate of interest. 
(x) Government has de-reserved the readymade garments, hosiery 
and knitwear from SSI sector so that large scale investments 
may be encouraged in these sectors. 
(xi) National Institute of Fashion Technology (NIFT) has been set up 
to provide the leadership role in sensitizing the Industry to the 
concept of value addition by including trained professionals to 
manage the industry. This has resulted in an increased demand 
for trained professionals in various sectors servicing the industry.

†2684. SHRI SHRIMATI MAYA SINGH: Will the Minister of RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
the details of two hundred districts selected under the Rural 
Employment Guarantee Programme introduced on 2nd February, 2006; 
the procedure adopted to select the districts from various States; 
and 
the way by which Ministry of Rural Development and Planning 
Commission have coordinated and the role of States in this programme? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRIMATI SURYAKANTA PATIL): (a)Alist of 200 districts 
identified for implementation of NREG Act in the first phase is given in the 
Statement-I [Refer to the Statement -I appended to answer to Unstarred 
question No. 2630] 
(b) and (c) Out of the 200 districts identified for implementation of NREGA 
in the first phase, 150 districts are those districts which had been earlier 
identified for NFFWP and 50 new districts have been identified by the Planning 
Commission. These 150 districts were selected on the basis of an exercise 
conducted by the Planning Commission on the basr nf three parameters 
SC/ST population, inverse of agricultural productivity per worker and ivnerse 
of agricultural wage rate. The States were given an extended list on the 
basis of above parameters and were given to indicate their choice out of the 
extended list and also suggest aniy other district with detailed justification. 
Least one district was selected fro m each State except Goa. For North 
Eastern States except Assam where data on above parameters was not 
available, districts, were selectejd out of RSVY districts. Out of the 50 new 
districts selected, 45 districts are those districts which were covered under 
Rashtriya Sam Vikas Yojana (RSVY) but not included in NFFWP. 5 districts 
have been identified by the Planning Commission to assess the impact of 
the programme in certain specific backgrounds. 
Every state is required to frame and notify a State Scheme under National 
Rural Employment Guarantee Act within six months of the commencement 
of the Act. This Scheme will be implemented and expenditure shared 
between the Centre and States as; per provisions of the Act.

Quality of drinking water in rural areas 
†2705. SHRI DILIP SINGH JUDEV: Will the Minister of RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
whether any proper arrangements have been made to check the 
quality of water supplied under hand- pump ground water scheme in rural 
areas; 
if so, the details thereof; 
the dates on which such arrangement has been reviewed to ensure 
its compliance and the dates on which the quality of water being provided 
in rural areas has been tested by the Central team; and 
the number of hand-pumps and ground water schemes in each State 
and the water received from which has been declared unfit for drinking the 
during last three years? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE JN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI A. NARENDRA) : (a) and (b) Drinking Water 
Supply is a State Subject. The Government of India renders financial and 
technical assistance to the States in  this endeavour through a centrally 
sponsored programme, namely, Accelerated Rural Water Supply 
Programme (ARWSP). Under the programme, the Union Government 
has been assisting the State Governments in developing an integrated 
system of drinking water quality monitoring by setting up of district level 
laboratories for water quality testing, reporting and generating awareness 
among rural masses about the importance of water quality and its relation 
to health. Executive Guidelines for setting up of district level water quality 
testing laboratories were issued in 1990. 100% Central assistance to 
the tune of Rs. 4.00 lakh (1.00 lakh for building and 3.00 lakh for equipment) 
to each such laboratory is admissible as per the existing guidelines. 
Operational Manual, which outlines the procedures for water quality testing 
was also issued. Till date, 459 district level water quality testing 
laboratories have been sanctioned by the Government of India and 386 
have been established, 146 have been established by State Governments 
and 14 by other organizations. These laboratories test the quality of 
hand-pump and ground water sources.

tests carried out by these laboratories. The programme of water quality 
monitoring and surveillance was reviewed recently and National Rural Drinking 
Water Quality Monitoring and Surveillance Programme for institutionalization 
of community participation has been launched in February 2006. Guidelines 
of the programme have also been issued to the State Governments. It is 
envisaged in this programme that grassroot level workers will be testing the 
quality of all drinking water sources with the help of user friendly field test 
kits. The district level laboratories will test positive samples.

concessional duty of 5% continues to be at 5% on most of the 
machinery items.
